question: What is the primary definition of disease surveillance in public health?

options.A: The immediate treatment of individual patients in an emergency room
options.B: The systematic, ongoing collection, analysis, and interpretation of health-related data
options.C: The mandatory quarantine of all travelers entering a country
options.D: The annual auditing of hospital financial accounts and budgets

explanation: Disease surveillance is defined as the systematic, ongoing collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data necessary for public health planning and action. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h1)

question: How does effective disease surveillance help public health systems?

options.A: It allows systems to transition from a reactive posture to proactive prevention
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for clinical nurses in hospitals
options.C: It focuses solely on financial gains for private healthcare facilities
options.D: It restricts communities from accessing essential health education

explanation: Continuous surveillance allows healthcare systems to detect health threats early and shift from a reactive approach to proactive prevention and planning. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h1)

question: Which of the following is a primary objective of public health surveillance?

options.A: To detect epidemics and monitor baseline disease endemicity
options.B: To increase the cost of pharmaceutical drugs
options.C: To diagnose and treat individual medical complications in a clinic
options.D: To replace traditional nursing documentation with automated software

explanation: Detecting epidemics, monitoring baseline disease rates, and evaluating control measures are core objectives of public health surveillance. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h2)

question: Why is tracking vaccine-preventable diseases an important surveillance objective in Nigeria?

options.A: To ensure that nurses receive higher administrative salaries
options.B: To track conditions like polio and measles and evaluate immunization success
options.C: To eliminate the need for community health extension workers
options.D: To prove that infectious diseases no longer exist in the region

explanation: Tracking diseases like polio and measles helps monitor the burden and evaluate the effectiveness of mass vaccination campaigns. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h2)

question: Which type of surveillance relies on healthcare providers routinely reporting cases without prompting from public health authorities?
explanation: Passive surveillance involves routine, unprompted reporting of notifiable diseases by healthcare providers to local or national authorities. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h3)

question: What is the primary characteristic of syndromic surveillance?

options.A: It relies exclusively on confirmed laboratory test results
options.B: It focuses on pre-diagnostic indicators like symptoms and school absenteeism for early warning
options.C: It is only conducted once every ten years during a national census
options.D: It mandates that every clinic in the country report daily financial status

explanation: Syndromic surveillance analyzes pre-diagnostic data such as clinical symptoms or absenteeism to detect unusual health events early. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h3)

question: What is the final and most critical step in the disease surveillance process?

options.B: Translating surveillance insights into public health action and interventions
options.C: Punishing clinics that report high disease rates
options.D: Filing data in locked cabinets without review

explanation: Action is the ultimate goal of surveillance, turning data insights into concrete public health interventions to protect the community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h4)

question: During the data analysis phase of surveillance, how is data typically aggregated to find patterns?

options.B: By patient hair color and shoe size
options.C: By hospital paint color and building height
options.D: By staff uniform type and shift schedule

explanation: Public health professionals analyze surveillance data by time, place, and person to identify epidemiological trends and anomalies. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h4)

question: Why are laboratory reports considered vital sources of health information in surveillance?

options.A: They provide microbiological confirmation of pathogens and track resistance
options.B: They determine the monthly salaries of hospital administrators
options.C: They replace the need for physical nursing assessments
options.D: They track patient financial insurance claims exclusively

explanation: Laboratory reports provide microbiological confirmation of diseases, which is essential for accurate diagnosis and tracking resistance patterns. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h5)

question: What is a major advantage of modern electronic and mHealth tools in disease surveillance?

options.A: They eliminate the need for any human involvement in healthcare
options.B: They enhance the speed and accuracy of data transmission
options.C: They guarantee that diseases will never occur again
options.D: They prevent patients from visiting primary health clinics

explanation: Electronic surveillance and mHealth applications significantly improve the speed and accuracy of transmitting health data from remote sites to central authorities. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h5)

question: When should disease control measures be implemented during an outbreak investigation?

options.A: Only after the outbreak has completely ended on its own
options.B: Immediately, even before the exact causative agent is fully identified
options.C: After waiting for international permission and funding approval
options.D: Only when media outlets begin reporting on the situation

explanation: Control measures should be implemented immediately to halt transmission, rather than waiting for exhaustive investigation results. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h6)

question: What is a key activity performed during descriptive epidemiology in an outbreak?

options.A: Analyzing cases by time, place, and person
options.B: Auditing the hospital cafeteria's food supply
options.C: Evaluating the architectural design of clinic buildings
options.D: Assessing the personal wealth of affected patients

explanation: Descriptive epidemiology involves characterizing outbreak cases by time, place, and person to understand how the disease is spreading. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h6)

question: Why are primary health care nurses considered frontline sentinels in disease surveillance?

options.A: They are the first healthcare professionals to encounter and identify suspected disease cases
options.B: They are solely responsible for writing national health policies
options.C: They work exclusively in high-level tertiary research laboratories
options.D: They manage the financial budgets of the Ministry of Health

explanation: Nurses at the primary health care level are frontline sentinels because they directly interact with patients and are first to spot unusual health conditions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h7)

question: Which of the following tasks is a key responsibility of community health nurses in surveillance?

options.A: Conducting contact tracing and educating families on disease prevention
options.B: Manufacturing pharmaceutical vaccines in industrial plants
options.C: Importing medical diagnostic equipment from overseas
options.D: Performing surgical operations independently in rural areas

explanation: Community health nurses engage in contact tracing, health education, and immunization to help control and prevent disease spread. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h7)

question: What is a primary cause of under-reporting in disease surveillance systems?

options.A: Excessive free time among clinical staff
options.B: Heavy clinical workloads and complicated reporting procedures
options.C: An overabundance of laboratory confirmation kits
options.D: Mandatory daily audits by international health organizations

explanation: Heavy workloads, staff shortages, and complex reporting procedures frequently contribute to under-reporting by busy clinicians. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h8)

question: How can stigma and cultural beliefs negatively impact disease surveillance?

options.A: By forcing communities to participate in mandatory vaccination drives
options.B: By deterring individuals from seeking care and causing hidden community outbreaks
options.C: By speeding up the transmission of electronic health records
options.D: By ensuring 100% accurate laboratory diagnosis for all patients

explanation: Stigma and fear of isolation can cause patients to avoid healthcare facilities, leading to hidden cases and delayed outbreak responses. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h8)
